title: AP Microeconomics
summary: Use marginal reasoning to analyse markets, firms, labour and policy trade-offs.
frameworkNote: 2026–27 structure checked against College Board on 15 October 2026: 6 units. Original VertexED focused lessons and self-check questions sample each unit; they do not replace the full course framework, required materials or teacher review.

modules.title: Marginal choices and trade-offs
modules.focus: Compare additional benefit with additional cost.
explanation: Economic choices depend on the next unit, not only total benefits or past spending. A rational choice expands an activity while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost, subject to constraints. Sunk costs cannot be recovered and should not determine future incremental choices.

A production possibilities frontier records feasible combinations. Its slope measures opportunity cost; a bowed-out shape represents increasing opportunity costs as resources move into less suitable uses. Trade can expand consumption possibilities without changing the production frontier.

workedExample.prompt: An extra study hour brings a benefit valued at 18 and a cost valued at 12.
steps: Compare incremental values: 18 exceeds 12.
The additional hour has positive net benefit of 6; earlier study hours are irrelevant to this marginal comparison.

misconception.claim: A large past investment means continuing is always sensible.
misconception.correction: Past unrecoverable costs do not change the future benefits and costs.

questions.prompt: An extra unit brings benefit 9 and cost 13. Should it be added under this rule?
questions.hint: Compare marginal values.
questions.answer: No. It reduces net benefit by 4.

questions.prompt: Why can opportunity cost rise along a bowed-out frontier?
questions.hint: Consider resource suitability.
questions.answer: Resources transferred later may be less suited to the expanding activity, so more of the other good must be forgone.

questions.hint: Evaluate the decision from now onward.
questions.prompt: A project already spent 100 irrecoverably. Finishing requires 30 more and produces benefit 45. Under the stated net-benefit objective, should it finish?
questions.answer: Yes. The incremental benefit exceeds the remaining cost by 15; the sunk 100 cannot be changed by this choice.
checkpoints: Choose completion based on +15 incremental benefit.
hints: Evaluate the decision from now onward.
Past irrecoverable spending occurs under either option.

questions.hint: No cash payment is needed for an opportunity cost.
questions.prompt: An extra unit has cash cost 4 and uses time worth 7 in the best alternative. Its benefit is 9. Should it be added under marginal net-benefit analysis?
questions.answer: No. Economic marginal cost is 4+7=11, exceeding benefit 9 by 2.
checkpoints: Include the opportunity cost of time.
Reject the unit because net benefit is −2.
hints: No cash payment is needed for an opportunity cost.
Compare benefit with the full economic cost.

notes.title: Reasoning through marginal choices and trade-offs
paragraphs: Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit and additional cost of one more unit, rather than average totals or money already irreversibly spent. A decision can be worthwhile at one scale and not at a larger scale because marginal benefits or costs change. Sunk costs do not change with the present choice and should not enter the incremental comparison, while opportunity costs include the value of the best forgone alternative even when no cash payment occurs. In a discrete problem, add units while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost under the stated objective, checking any fixed costs that are still avoidable.

workedExamples.prompt: A learner’s benefits from three extra practice sessions are 20, 14 and 8 units, each costing 10 units of time value. How many should be added?
steps: Net marginal benefits are +10, +4 and −2, so the first two improve the stated objective and the third reduces it.
The best additional plan is two sessions, giving total benefit 34 and cost 20.
workedExamples.conclusion: Two additional sessions yield the greatest net benefit, 14 units.

flashcards.front: What is a marginal cost?
flashcards.back: The additional cost of one more unit.

flashcards.front: What is a sunk cost?
flashcards.back: A past cost that cannot be recovered or changed by the current choice.

flashcards.front: Why include opportunity cost?
flashcards.back: A choice sacrifices the best available alternative.

flashcards.front: Why can averages mislead?
flashcards.back: They can hide whether the next unit adds more cost than benefit.

modules.title: Market changes and elasticity
modules.focus: Separate movements along curves from shifts.
explanation: Demand describes quantities buyers want at different prices, holding other factors constant. Supply describes sellers’ quantities. A good’s own price causes movement along a curve; income, tastes, input costs and technology can shift curves.

Price elasticity measures responsiveness using percentage changes. If demand is inelastic, a price rise increases total revenue, other things equal, because the proportional quantity decline is smaller. Tax incidence also depends on relative responsiveness, not who sends the payment.

workedExample.prompt: Price rises 10% and quantity demanded falls 4%. Interpret elasticity.
steps: The magnitude is 4 ÷ 10 = 0.4.
Demand is inelastic over this change, so revenue rises approximately under the stated changes.

misconception.claim: A higher price shifts the demand curve left.
misconception.correction: It causes a movement along a fixed demand curve; a non-price determinant shifts demand.

questions.prompt: What happens to equilibrium price and quantity if production costs fall?
questions.hint: Shift supply right while demand stays fixed.
questions.answer: Price falls and quantity rises in the standard upward-supply, downward-demand model.

questions.prompt: Which side bears more tax burden when demand is less elastic than supply?
questions.hint: Consider who changes behaviour less.
questions.answer: Buyers bear more because their quantity response is relatively smaller.

questions.hint: Ignore the negative sign only when reporting magnitude.
questions.prompt: Demand quantity rises 12% after price falls 6%. Find elasticity magnitude and classify it.
questions.answer: Elasticity magnitude is 12/6=2, so demand is elastic.
checkpoints: Classify elastic because it exceeds one.
hints: Ignore the negative sign only when reporting magnitude.
Compare the magnitude with one.

questions.hint: Ask which side can reduce participation more easily.
questions.prompt: A per-unit tax is legally collected from sellers. Demand is nearly perfectly inelastic and supply is elastic. Who likely bears most economic burden, and why?
questions.answer: Buyers likely bear most because their quantity demanded responds little to price; legal collection from sellers does not determine economic incidence.
checkpoints: Explain why that side bears more.
hints: Ask which side can reduce participation more easily.
Incidence depends on relative elasticities.

notes.title: Reasoning through market changes and elasticity
paragraphs: A movement along demand results from a change in the good’s own price, whereas a demand shift comes from another determinant such as income, tastes or a related good’s price. Supply shifts reflect changes such as input costs or technology. Elasticity measures percentage responsiveness and avoids dependence on the measurement units of quantity. For demand, the magnitude is usually reported positively even though price and quantity demanded move oppositely. Tax incidence depends on relative elasticities rather than who physically sends the tax payment: the less responsive side has less ability to avoid the transaction and tends to bear more burden.

workedExamples.prompt: Price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80. Use midpoint elasticity.
steps: Quantity percentage change is −20/90≈−22.22%; price percentage change is 2/11≈18.18%.
Elasticity magnitude is 22.22/18.18≈1.22, so demand is elastic over this interval.
workedExamples.conclusion: Midpoint demand elasticity is about 1.22 in magnitude.

flashcards.front: What causes movement along a demand curve?
flashcards.back: A change in the good’s own price.

flashcards.front: What does elasticity compare?
flashcards.back: Percentage quantity response with percentage change in its determinant.

flashcards.front: Who bears more tax burden when relatively less elastic?
flashcards.back: The side less responsive to price.

flashcards.front: Why use midpoint percentages?
flashcards.back: They give the same interval elasticity whichever direction is considered.

modules.title: Costs and competitive production
modules.focus: Choose output and shutdown decisions using different comparisons.
explanation: A competitive firm takes market price as given, so marginal revenue equals price. It selects an output with rising marginal cost equal to marginal revenue, provided producing covers variable cost. Profit then depends on the difference between price and average total cost.

In the short run, fixed costs remain even during shutdown. A firm may operate with losses if revenue covers variable costs; the long-run exit decision considers all costs. Distinguish accounting profit from economic profit, which includes implicit opportunity costs.

workedExample.prompt: At the chosen output of 20, price is 8, average variable cost 5 and average total cost 10.
steps: Operating covers variable costs and contributes 60 towards fixed costs, so it can minimise short-run loss.

misconception.claim: Any loss-making firm must shut down immediately.
misconception.correction: Production can reduce short-run losses when price covers average variable cost.

questions.prompt: At output 30, price is 12 and average total cost 9. Calculate profit.
questions.hint: Multiply the per-unit margin.

questions.prompt: Why is zero economic profit compatible with staying in business?
questions.hint: Remember implicit costs.
questions.answer: Revenue covers explicit costs and the opportunity costs of the owner’s resources, including a normal return.

questions.hint: Convert the average variable cost into a total.
questions.prompt: At output 50, price is 8, AVC is 5 and fixed cost is 100. Find profit.
questions.answer: Revenue is 400; variable cost is 250; total cost is 350; profit is 50.
hints: Convert the average variable cost into a total.
Add fixed cost once.

questions.hint: Compare producing with the zero-output alternative.
questions.prompt: A firm’s price is below its minimum AVC and all variable costs are avoidable by shutting down. Why should it shut down in the short run?
questions.answer: At any positive output, revenue cannot cover variable costs, so production adds to the unavoidable fixed-cost loss; shutdown avoids those extra losses.
checkpoints: Explain the reduction in loss from shutdown.
hints: Compare producing with the zero-output alternative.
Do not claim shutdown removes unavoidable fixed costs.

notes.title: Reasoning through costs and competitive production
paragraphs: Profit compares total revenue with all economic costs, including opportunity costs. In perfect competition, a price-taking firm chooses output where marginal cost equals price on the appropriate rising portion, provided producing is better than shutting down. The short-run shutdown comparison uses avoidable variable costs: revenue that covers variable costs and part of fixed cost can reduce losses. Long-run exit also considers fixed costs that become avoidable. Average total cost determines profit per unit at the chosen output, while marginal cost determines the incremental output decision. Confusing these roles can produce a correct-looking profit calculation at the wrong quantity.

workedExamples.prompt: A competitive firm sells 40 units at price 9. AVC is 6 and ATC is 11. Find profit and compare producing with short-run shutdown, assuming fixed costs cannot be avoided.
steps: Producing yields contribution (9−6)×40=120 towards fixed costs; shutdown loses the full 200, so producing limits the loss to 80.
workedExamples.conclusion: The firm loses 80 but prefers producing at this candidate output to shutting down under the assumptions.

flashcards.front: What determines profit per unit?
flashcards.back: Price minus average total cost.

flashcards.front: What does marginal cost help determine?
flashcards.back: The best incremental output choice.

flashcards.front: What is the basic short-run shutdown comparison?
flashcards.back: Revenue versus avoidable variable cost.

flashcards.front: Why can a loss-making firm still produce?
flashcards.back: It may cover variable cost and part of unavoidable fixed cost.

modules.title: Market power and strategic interaction
modules.focus: Identify why price can exceed marginal cost.
explanation: A monopolist faces the market demand curve. Selling more generally requires a lower price, so marginal revenue lies below demand. It chooses output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, then reads price from demand rather than from marginal revenue.

Oligopoly decisions depend on rivals’ choices. A dominant strategy is best regardless of the other player’s action; a Nash equilibrium is a combination where no player benefits from changing alone. A dominant strategy need not exist.

workedExample.prompt: A monopolist’s profit-maximising quantity is 10; demand gives price 15 and average cost is 9.
steps: Read the selling price from demand at quantity 10.

misconception.claim: A monopolist can set any price and sell any quantity.
misconception.correction: The demand curve constrains the combinations buyers will purchase.

questions.prompt: Why can monopoly create deadweight loss relative to competition?
questions.hint: Compare marginal benefit and cost.
questions.answer: Restricted output leaves some units unproduced even though buyers’ marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.

questions.prompt: Does a Nash equilibrium guarantee the highest combined payoff?
questions.hint: Separate individual incentives from joint results.
questions.answer: No. Neither player may gain by changing alone even when coordinated choices would yield greater combined payoff.

questions.hint: Quantity comes from marginal comparison.
questions.prompt: Demand is P=30−Q and MR=30−2Q. Constant MC is 10. Find monopoly quantity and price.
questions.answer: Q=10 from 30−2Q=10; P=20 from demand.
hints: Quantity comes from marginal comparison.
Price comes from buyers’ demand.

questions.hint: Hold the other player’s action fixed when testing equilibrium.
questions.prompt: Two firms each earn 5 if both choose A and 3 if both choose B. If one chooses B while the other chooses A, the B chooser earns 6 and the A chooser 1. Is (B,B) a Nash equilibrium and is it jointly best?
questions.answer: Yes: deviating from B to A against B lowers own payoff from 3 to 1. It is not jointly best, since (A,A) gives total 10 rather than 6.
checkpoints: Check a unilateral deviation against B.
hints: Hold the other player’s action fixed when testing equilibrium.
Joint payoff is a separate comparison.

notes.title: Reasoning through market power and strategic interaction
paragraphs: A monopolist faces the market demand curve, so selling additional units can require a lower price on units already sold. Marginal revenue therefore lies below demand in the standard single-price downward-sloping model. The firm first selects quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, then uses demand to find the price buyers will pay. Monopoly profit is not guaranteed: average cost can exceed that price. In strategic settings, a Nash equilibrium means each player’s action is a best response to others, not that the outcome maximises combined welfare. Always read the payoff order before comparing unilateral deviations.

workedExamples.prompt: A monopolist has demand P=20−Q, marginal revenue MR=20−2Q and constant marginal cost 4. Find optimal quantity and price under the interior-profit-maximisation model.
steps: Set MR=MC: 20−2Q=4, so Q=8.
Use demand, not MR, for price: P=20−8=12.
workedExamples.conclusion: The model selects quantity 8 and price 12.

flashcards.front: Why can MR lie below price for a monopolist?
flashcards.back: Selling more can require reducing the price on earlier units.

flashcards.front: Which curve gives price after selecting monopoly quantity?
flashcards.back: Demand.

flashcards.front: Does monopoly guarantee positive profit?
flashcards.back: No; costs can exceed revenue.

flashcards.front: What defines a Nash equilibrium?
flashcards.back: No player benefits from a unilateral action change given others’ choices.

modules.title: Labour demand and factor payments
modules.focus: Connect a worker’s additional output to revenue.
explanation: Demand for labour is derived from demand for the output workers produce. In a competitive output market, marginal revenue product equals marginal product multiplied by product price. A competitive employer hires until marginal revenue product meets the wage, under standard assumptions.

Changes in productivity or output price shift labour demand. A monopsonistic employer faces an upward-sloping labour supply and a marginal hiring cost above the wage when raising wages for all workers, leading to different employment and pay outcomes.

workedExample.prompt: An additional worker makes 6 extra units sold at 4 each in a competitive product market.
steps: Marginal revenue product is 6 × 4 = 24.
Hiring is worthwhile at a marginal employment cost below 24, other things equal.

misconception.claim: Labour demand depends only on the number of people seeking work.
misconception.correction: Employers’ demand reflects productivity and the value of resulting output.

questions.prompt: Productivity rises with product price unchanged. What happens to labour demand?
questions.hint: Use marginal revenue product.
questions.answer: It shifts right because additional workers generate more revenue at each employment level.

questions.prompt: Why can a monopsonist’s marginal hiring cost exceed the wage?
questions.hint: Consider existing employees.
questions.answer: Hiring an extra worker may require raising wages for workers already employed as well as paying the new worker.

questions.hint: Use the competitive price as marginal revenue.
questions.prompt: An additional worker produces 7 units sold at 6 each in a competitive output market. The worker costs 40. Find MRP and the incremental profit change.
questions.answer: MRP=7×6=42; incremental profit is 42−40=2.
hints: Use the competitive price as marginal revenue.
Compare increments rather than total firm profit.

questions.hint: Include the four existing workers’ wage increases.
questions.prompt: A monopsonist pays all workers the same wage. Four workers each receive 10, but hiring a fifth requires paying all five 11. Find marginal hiring cost.
questions.answer: Total wage cost rises from 40 to 55, so marginal hiring cost is 15, exceeding the new worker’s wage of 11.
checkpoints: Subtract to obtain 15 and explain the existing-worker raises.
hints: Include the four existing workers’ wage increases.
Marginal cost is the change in total cost.

notes.title: Reasoning through labour demand and factor payments
paragraphs: Labour demand is derived from the value of additional output workers help produce. In a competitive product market, marginal revenue product is marginal product multiplied by the output price. A profit-maximising competitive employer compares this value with the wage for an additional worker, recognising that productivity can change as employment increases. Product-market power requires marginal revenue rather than price in the value calculation. In a simple monopsony with one wage paid to all workers, hiring another worker can require raising wages for existing workers, making marginal hiring cost exceed the wage itself. Institutional details can change these simplified relationships.

workedExamples.prompt: A firm sells output at 5 per unit. Successive workers add 8, 6 and 4 units, and each costs a wage of 25. How many are worthwhile at the margin?
steps: Marginal revenue products are 40, 30 and 20.
The first two exceed wage 25, while the third does not; hire two under the stated discrete model.
workedExamples.conclusion: Two workers pass the marginal value-versus-wage test.

flashcards.front: Why is labour demand called derived demand?
flashcards.back: It comes from demand for the output labour helps produce.

flashcards.front: What is MRP in a competitive output market?
flashcards.back: Marginal product times output price.

flashcards.front: What happens when product price rises, other things equal?
flashcards.back: Marginal revenue product and labour demand rise.

flashcards.front: Why can monopsony marginal hiring cost exceed wage?
flashcards.back: Hiring can require raising wages paid to existing workers too.

modules.title: Externalities, public goods and policy
modules.focus: Compare private incentives with social costs and benefits.
explanation: An externality affects people outside a transaction without being fully reflected in its price. Negative production externalities make social marginal cost exceed private marginal cost, so an unregulated market may produce too much relative to the efficient quantity.

Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, creating free-rider incentives. Policy may use taxes, subsidies, rules or public provision, but evaluation should include information needs, enforcement costs and distribution rather than assuming every intervention succeeds.

workedExample.prompt: A unit costs its producer 5 but imposes external damage of 2.
steps: Social marginal cost is 5 + 2 = 7.
A corrective charge matching marginal external damage can align incentives in the idealised model.

misconception.claim: Any government-provided service is a public good.
misconception.correction: The classification depends on rivalry and excludability, not ownership.

questions.prompt: Why might a vaccination generate a positive externality?
questions.hint: Consider effects on others.
questions.answer: Reduced transmission can benefit other people beyond the vaccinated individual, when the vaccine reduces transmission.

questions.prompt: Why can free riding reduce private provision of a public good?
questions.hint: Think about payment incentives.
questions.answer: People can benefit without paying, so voluntary revenue may be insufficient to fund the socially valuable quantity.

questions.hint: The tax targets the gap, not the whole social cost.
questions.prompt: An activity has private marginal cost 8 and external marginal cost 3. Find social marginal cost and the corrective tax in the simple constant-damage model.
questions.answer: Social marginal cost is 11; a per-unit tax of 3 makes the private decision face that cost, under the model assumptions.
checkpoints: Identify tax equal to marginal damage.
hints: The tax targets the gap, not the whole social cost.
Keep the constant-damage assumption.

questions.hint: Ask whether one user reduces what remains for others.
questions.prompt: Classify an open-access fishery and a noncongested public warning signal as common resource or public good, explaining rivalry.
questions.answer: The fishery is a common resource because catching fish reduces the stock available to others. The warning signal is a public good in the stated setting because one person receiving it does not reduce others’ access, and exclusion is difficult.
checkpoints: Apply the common-resource versus public-good distinction with exclusion assumptions.
hints: Ask whether one user reduces what remains for others.
Do not equate all shared things with public goods.

notes.title: Reasoning through externalities, public goods and policy
paragraphs: An externality occurs when a decision creates costs or benefits for others that are not fully reflected in the decision-maker’s incentives. With a negative production externality, marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost; the unregulated competitive outcome can produce too much relative to the social optimum. A corrective tax can align incentives when its design reflects the relevant marginal damage, but information and enforcement matter. Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable in the relevant setting, creating free-rider problems. These features differ from common resources, which are difficult to exclude users from but are rival in use.

workedExamples.prompt: Demand gives marginal benefit MB=20−Q, private marginal cost is 4 and external marginal damage is 2 per unit. Find market and socially efficient quantities.
steps: The market sets MB=private MC: 20−Q=4, so Q=16.
Social MC is 4+2=6; efficiency sets 20−Q=6, so Q=14. A tax of 2 per unit aligns the marginal costs in this model.
workedExamples.conclusion: The market quantity is 16 and the efficient quantity is 14.

flashcards.front: What is marginal social cost with external damage?
flashcards.back: Private marginal cost plus marginal external cost.

flashcards.front: What two features define a public good?
flashcards.back: Nonrivalry and nonexcludability.

flashcards.front: How does a common resource differ?
flashcards.back: It is rival despite difficult exclusion.

flashcards.front: What is free riding?
flashcards.back: Benefiting without contributing to provision when exclusion is difficult.
